newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Wave of criticism hits Australian race row politician.
newsitem.headline: Wave of criticism hits Australian race row politician.

text.p: Independent Australian race row politician Pauline Hanson was submerged under a tidal wave of criticism on Sunday as politicians, demonstrators and business leaders attacked her policies as divisive and ignorant.
The criticism followed an ugly protest in Western Australia state where tomatoes, eggs and insults were hurled at Hanson as she arrived for a fund-raising breakfast in Perth.
Hanson, who sparked a bitter national race debate last year, was surrounded by police and security guards and was unhurt.
Three protesters in a crowd of about 500 raised an Aboriginal flag. Others shouted insults such as "racist scum".
Australian media speculated on Sunday that conservative Prime Minister John Howard would make his first formal repudiation of Hanson's policies in a speech later in the week.
Former Australian prime minister Malcolm Fraser joined a host of serving ministers in attacking Hanson's policy of restricted immigration as repugnant and offensive.
"One thing is certain, her white, Anglo-Celtic caucasian Australia would become full of racial discord and bitterness," Fraser told reporters at a book launch.

Opinion polls last week showed Hanson is rapidly attracting an increasing number of voters disillusioned with major parties, with one poll showing about 10 percent of electors would vote for Hanson's One Nation party.
Treasurer Peter Costello said on Sunday Hanson's policies were divisive and notable only for their paucity of ideas.
"She has no plan for Australia and the divisive and vicious future that she is promulgating will be repudiated," Costello told the Channel Seven television network.
Environment Minister Robert Hill said Hanson's One Nation party had yet to produce credible alternative policies and doubted it would ever gain a significant presence in parliament.

"Most Australians, when they come to voting in an election, actually ask what are the positive alternatives," Hill, who is also government leader in the Senate, said in a television interview. "You can run this fear campaign only for so long."

Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer said last week Hanson threatened Australia's increasing income from trade with its Asian neighbours. Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said her stand of banning foreign investment and her racist immigration policy could cost tens of thousands of Australian jobs.
Police estimated about 2,000 protesters surrounded a stadium in Perth on Saturday where Hanson addressed a rally of about 1,000 supporters.
Australian newspapers also reported on Saturday that the McDonald's fast food chain had changed its mind about asking Hanson to appear in a Perth store for a charity promotion.
Opposition regional development spokesman Simon Crean said cultural diversity had made Australia great.
"What she stands for, draped in the Australian flag, is very un-Australian. It's based on bigotry, it's based on division," Crean said in a television interview.
Hanson sparked a divisive national race row last year when she warned Australia was in danger of being over-run by Asians and complained that Aborigines were given special treatment.
